key_concept: Mole-to-mole stoichiometry from a balanced combustion equation: each mole of $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}$ gives 4 moles of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (conservation of carbon atoms).
steps: Find the molar mass of n-butane: $M(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}) = 4(12) + 10(1) = 58\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.
Apply the mole ratio $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}} : \mathrm{CO_2} = 1 : 4$. This gives $n(\mathrm{CO_2}) = 2 \times 4 = 8\ \mathrm{mol}$.
why_not_others: 176 g results from using the wrong ratio, for example 1 mol butane giving 4 mol $\mathrm{CO_2}$ while treating 116 g as only 1 mol, or halving the answer by misreading the coefficients 2 : 8. The values 322 g and 362 g do not correspond to any whole-number mole count of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ ($44n$), so they are distractors.
common_trap: Reading the coefficients of the balanced equation (2 : 8) as a 1 : 8 ratio, or forgetting to convert grams to moles before applying the ratio.
time_saving_tip: Skip balancing the full equation and use carbon conservation: each $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}$ gives 4 $\mathrm{CO_2}$. So the mass of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is $\frac{116}{58} \times 4 \times 44 = 352\ \mathrm{g}$.
